unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Unit 5 is about action and movement: how people and animals move, how we describe fast and slow actions, and how we make good choices when we feel excited or under pressure. You will read about a runner who learns to accelerate, animals that gallop, squeeze and spiral, and three children who rescue a lost dog. You will meet strong verbs such as squeeze, peek, proceed and defend, and you will learn to say exactly how an action happens — quickly, slowly or carefully. Everything leads to this unit’s adventure story, “The Spiral Cave”.
unit.learningPath:
Start with the Vocabulary section. Learn a few action words each day and use each one in a sentence.
Work through the six grammar lessons: past simple, adjective + noun phrases, adverbs of manner, imperatives and modals, sequencing words, and proofreading.
Read the four texts, including the story “The Spiral Cave”, and answer the comprehension questions.
Work through Speaking, Writing and Activities, then take the Action and Movement checkpoint quiz.
Finish with the self-assessment. If you have access to live teacher sessions, bring your recordings and writing to share there — this is optional, since the checkpoint quiz and self-assessment already show what you have learned.

readings.title: The Race at the Village Field
readings.setting: A village sports field on a Saturday morning
readings.passageScript:
On Saturday morning, the whole village gathered at the field for the running race. Amal stood at the starting line and felt a rush of pressure, because her family, her friends and even little children from the next street had come to watch. She checked her shoelaces twice and took a deep breath to stay calm.
When Teacher Yasmin blew her whistle, the runners set off together. At first Amal ran slowly, saving her energy for the long stretch ahead. Then, as the finish line came into view, she began to accelerate. Her heart rate grew faster and faster, and the sound of her own breathing filled her ears.
In the next field, a horse began to gallop beside the fence, as if it wanted to join the race. Amal did not look back or let it distract her. She ran quickly but carefully, remembering to watch her footing on the uneven grass.
She crossed the finish line first, with her arms high in the air. The crowd cheered, and her little brother waved a homemade flag.
“Well done,” said Teacher Yasmin, smiling. “You stayed calm under pressure, and you paced yourself perfectly. That is exactly how a good runner races.”
Amal grinned. She could not wait to tell her friends about the horse that had almost joined her race.

readings.title: How Animals Move
readings.setting: Grassland, gardens and rivers where animals live
readings.passageScript:
Animals move in many different ways, and each way helps them live safely in their world. A horse can gallop swiftly across open grass, using its long legs to cover ground fast when it needs to escape danger or simply enjoys running free. A snail, on the other hand, moves slowly and steadily, tracing a spiral shape into its shell as it grows.
Some animals move by squeezing their bodies into tiny spaces. A cat will squeeze through a narrow gap in a fence, bending its flexible body to fit through openings that look far too small.
Birds often move as a group, and they rely on signals to stay safe. When one bird spots danger, it may give a signal to warn the others, and the whole flock will quickly fly away together to prevent being caught by a predator.
Water is important for movement too. Some animals suffer when there is no water nearby, so they must move far, sometimes for many days, to find a river or a pool where they can drink and rest.
Watching how different animals move can excite us and teach us a great deal about the world we share. Whether an animal gallops, spirals, squeezes or signals to its group, every movement has its own purpose in nature.

readings.title: The Lost Goat (script)
readings.setting: The lanes and shops around the village market
readings.passageScript:
“Yesterday, Adam lost his little goat near the market. One moment she was tied by the well, and the next moment the rope was empty. Adam’s heart raced as he looked all around.
He began to gaze in every direction, hoping to spot her white coat among the market stalls. ‘I must find her before dark,’ he said quietly to himself.
He decided to check behind the shops first, where the goat sometimes liked to hide from the midday sun. First he took a quick peek into the narrow alley, moving fast because he was worried, not because he wanted to admire the view. Nothing there.
Then he proceeded slowly along the lane behind the bakery, listening carefully for any sound.
Suddenly he heard a soft sound, like a gentle bleat coming from behind some crates. Adam’s pressure eased at once.
There was the goat, calmly chewing on a piece of straw!
Adam ran to rescue her, scooping her up before she could wander off again. ‘I will always defend you,’ he said, hugging her close. ‘You gave me such a fright.’
He carried her home along the quiet lanes, promising himself he would check the rope twice from now on, so she would never wander away again.”

readings.title: The Spiral Cave
readings.setting: A forest-edge village beside a river, near an old tunnel
readings.passageScript:
One afternoon, three children were playing beside the river. Amal, Leo and Nora lived in a quiet village near the forest. They often made up games and told stories, but today they found something strange. Behind a pile of rocks, there was a dark hole in the ground.
“Let me peek inside!” said Leo.
Nora held his hand. “Be careful. It might not be safe.”
But Amal had already taken a step forward. “It is dark, but I can see something. The floor goes down in a spiral.”
“Like a staircase?” asked Leo.
“Yes! Let us explore it!” said Amal, feeling excited.
The children looked around for a strong stick and a torch. “We must check that it is safe,” said Nora. “We do not want to fall.”
They went in slowly. “First, peek inside. Then, proceed carefully,” whispered Amal, copying what their teacher always said in science class.
Inside, the air was cold. The spiral tunnel turned and turned. Leo pointed to the wall. “Look! A drawing of people… and a lion?”
They kept walking until they reached a wider space. “It is a cave!” shouted Nora. Their voices echoed off the stone.
Suddenly, they heard a soft sound.
“Was that a whistle?” asked Amal.
“No,” said Leo. “That was an animal!”
Then, out of the shadows, two eyes appeared. A small dog — thin and shivering — stepped forward. It wagged its tail.
“It looks hungry,” said Nora. “We have to rescue it!”
Amal reached into her bag and pulled out a piece of bread. She called gently to the dog. “Come here, boy.”
The dog sniffed and walked closer. “I think he is friendly,” said Leo. “He does not want to hurt us.”
“We should give him a name,” said Amal.
“Not yet,” said Nora. “First we need to check that he is not sick.”
The children carried the dog out of the cave. Outside, the sun was low in the sky.
“We must accelerate,” said Leo. “It is getting late!”
Back in the village, they went to the animal helper, Talia. She was kind and wise.
“Where did you find him?” she asked.
“In a spiral tunnel near the river,” said Amal.
“You were lucky,” said Talia. “That tunnel is very old. There is pressure from the soil above it. It could fall in at any time.”
“We did not know,” said Nora. “We were too excited.”
“Next time you must tell your parents first,” she said. “But I am glad you brought him to me.”
The dog was given clean water and food. He wagged his tail and let Nora squeeze his paw gently.
“He is strong,” said Talia. “He only needs rest.”
“But who left him there?” asked Leo.
“We may never know,” said Talia. “Sometimes people are greedy. They want an animal but do not care for it. That is not right. An animal like this can suffer when no one looks after it.”
The children were quiet. They did not like the thought of anyone being so unkind.
“We can help him,” said Nora. “Let us make posters and describe him. Someone might be looking for him.”
“That is a kind plan,” said Talia.
That night, Amal wrote in her notebook:
“We found a cave, a spiral path and a small dog. We learned to move slowly and to think. We felt pressure and fear, but we stayed strong.”
The next day, the children shared their story at school. Their teacher smiled. “You followed instructions, stayed calm and made good choices. That is something to be proud of.”
“What should we name him now?” asked Leo.
“How about Simba?” said Nora. “He is strong, like a lion.”
“Perfect,” said Amal. “He is our little rescued dog with a lion’s heart.”
Simba barked — happy, and safe at last.

grammar.title: Past Simple Tense
grammar.explanation: The past simple tense talks about actions that already happened and are finished. It lets us tell stories about the past, such as what we did yesterday or last week, as in “She rescued the bird yesterday” and “They galloped across the field”.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Regular verbs add -ed to the base verb: play becomes played, check becomes checked, gallop becomes galloped.
Irregular verbs change in their own way: go becomes went, run becomes ran, find becomes found, eat becomes ate.
The pattern is subject + past verb + when: “We found a cave last Saturday.”
For the negative, use did not + base verb: “She did not rescue the bird.”
For a question, use Did + subject + base verb: “Did she rescue the bird?”
grammar.commonMistake: It is easy to leave the base verb alone, as in “Yesterday she rescue the bird”. The word yesterday needs a past ending, so write “Yesterday she rescued the bird”. Irregular verbs change shape instead, so “I goed” becomes “I went”.
grammar.memoryTip: Tell yourself “Yesterday is history!” If the action is finished, the verb changes, and usually that change is -ed.
grammar.practice:

grammar.title: Adjective + Noun Phrases
grammar.explanation: An adjective describes something and a noun names a person, place or thing. Putting the adjective in front of the noun builds a clearer, more interesting phrase, such as “a greedy fox” or “a spiral staircase”.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Choose a describing word: greedy, spiral, hungry, shiny, tall.
Choose a naming word: fox, staircase, dog, car, tree.
Put the adjective first: a greedy fox, a spiral staircase, a shiny car.
Choose a / an by the sound that follows: a greedy fox, but an exciting race.
With two adjectives keep it short: “a big blue ball”, never a long list.
grammar.commonMistake: Writing “a fox greedy” places the describing word too late for English word order. Slide it in front and the phrase works: “a greedy fox”.
grammar.memoryTip: Adjectives are helpers that stand at the front of the queue. Describe it first, then name it — greedy fox!

grammar.title: Adverbs of Manner
grammar.explanation: An adverb of manner tells us how an action happens. Because this unit is all about action and movement, these words make your sentences come alive, as in “The horse galloped quickly” and “We walked carefully into the cave”.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Most adverbs of manner add -ly to an adjective: slow becomes slowly, quick becomes quickly, quiet becomes quietly.
If the adjective ends in -y, change the y to i and add -ly: happy becomes happily, easy becomes easily.
The adverb usually follows the verb: “She ran quickly.” “He spoke softly.”
A few are irregular, so good becomes well: “He plays football well.”
Two adverbs can share one verb when you join them: she ran quickly but carefully.
grammar.commonMistake: Saying “The snail moved slow” uses a describing word where a how word belongs. Reach for the -ly form instead: “The snail moved slowly”.
grammar.memoryTip: If the word answers the question “How?”, it usually ends in -ly. How did she run? Quickly!

grammar.title: Imperatives and Modal Verbs (can / must)
grammar.explanation: An imperative gives an instruction or a command, which is exactly what a how-to guide needs. A modal verb such as can or must adds what is possible or what is important, as in “Check your work!” and “You must be careful”.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Imperative: begin with the base verb and use no subject at all: “Proceed carefully.” “Peek inside.”
For a negative instruction add don’t: “Don’t run near the cave.”
can means able to or possible: “A horse can gallop.”
must means it is important or it is a rule: “You must check that it is safe.”
After can and must the verb keeps its plain form, so we write can gallop and never can gallops.
grammar.commonMistake: Two slips are common: “You must to check the cave” and “A bird can whistles”. Drop the extra to and keep the plain verb: “You must check the cave” and “A bird can whistle”.
grammar.memoryTip: After can and must, the verb stays plain — can go, must stop. An imperative jumps straight to the action, with no name in front of it.

grammar.title: Sequencing Words in a How-To Guide
grammar.explanation: Sequencing words show the order of the steps so a reader can follow instructions without getting lost. They hold a how-to guide together, and this unit asks you to write one about rescuing a lost animal.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Open with First to name the very first step: “First, move slowly so you do not frighten the animal.”
Use Then and After that for the middle steps: “Then, check that the animal is not hurt.”
Save Finally for the last step: “Finally, carry the animal to a helper.”
Put a comma after the sequencing word when it opens the sentence.
Pair every sequencing word with an imperative verb: Move, Check, Proceed, Carry.
grammar.commonMistake: Beginning every step with Then leaves the reader unsure which step comes last. Spread the signposts out instead, so the guide runs First, Then, After that, Finally.
grammar.memoryTip: Count the steps on four fingers — First, Then, After that, Finally — and give each finger one instruction.

grammar.title: Proofread Your Action Writing

grammar.ruleAndExamples:

writing.modelText: First, move slowly so you do not frighten the animal. Then, check that it is not hurt. After that, offer a little water. Finally, carry it to an adult helper who can look after it.

items: First, move slowly and quietly so you do not startle the animal.
Then, check the animal carefully for any injuries before you go any closer.
After that, proceed with care and offer it a little food or water.
Finally, carry the animal to a safe, sheltered spot away from danger.
Safety line: Always fetch an adult before you go near a lost animal.

writing.successCriteria: Every step starts with an imperative; the four sequencing words appear in order; a safety line names an adult; end punctuation is correct
writing.support: Act the rescue out first, then write down what your hands did at each moment.
writing.extension: Add a warning box explaining one thing a reader must never do.

writing.title: Writing 2: An Exciting Adventure
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write a short story of six to ten sentences about an exciting adventure.
Someone in your story must move quickly and then make a good choice.
Keep the past simple tense from beginning to end: rescued, galloped, ran, found.
Use at least five words from your Word Wall and underline each one.
writing.modelText: The gate swung open and the pony galloped past me. I checked the field, then ran to close the second gate. My heart rate raced, but I stayed calm and fetched my neighbour.
writing.expectedLength: Six to ten sentences in one paragraph

items: Last Saturday, without any warning, the neighbour's dog escaped through the gate.
I heard hooves and turned to see a pony that had also broken free and _galloped_ down the lane.
My heart raced with _pressure_ as I watched it head straight for the busy road.
I blew a loud _whistle_ that Baba had given me, hoping it would make the pony stop.
The pony slowed down and turned back towards the field instead.
I ran quickly to close the gate before it could _accelerate_ again.
Then I decided to _rescue_ the dog too, so I called it gently by name.
It felt exciting, but I made a good choice and stayed calm: I fetched my neighbour instead of chasing the animals alone.

writing.successCriteria: Every verb is past simple; five Word Wall words are underlined; the good choice is clear; sentences are punctuated correctly
writing.support: Plan three boxes: what happened, what went wrong, what good choice was made.
writing.extension: Add a line of direct speech, punctuated with speech marks.

writing.title: Writing 3: If I Had Found the Cave
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Imagine you found the spiral cave with Amal, Leo and Nora.
Write four sentences about what you would have done inside the tunnel.
Use the past simple tense throughout: I walked, I checked, I proceeded.
Include at least two words from the Vocabulary section.
writing.modelText: I peeked into the dark hole and waited for my eyes to adjust. Then I checked the walls before I proceeded down the spiral path.
writing.sentenceStarter: I peeked into the tunnel and then

items: I peeked into the dark hole and waited for my eyes to adjust to the shadows.
I checked the walls carefully before I proceeded down the spiral path.
I listened for any sound and gripped the torch tightly as I walked.
I found the frightened dog first and called to it gently so it would not run away.
otherAnswers: I would have stayed close to Nora and let her hold the torch steady while I looked for footprints.
I would have called out first to check whether anyone else was already inside the tunnel.
I would have drawn a quick sketch of the spiral path so we could find our way back out.

writing.successCriteria: All four sentences are past simple; two unit words are used correctly; each sentence has a capital letter and end punctuation
writing.support: Reread the cave paragraphs and list the verbs before you begin.
writing.extension: Add a fifth sentence saying how you felt, with an -ly adverb.

writing.title: Writing 4: How Animals Move Fact File
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write a heading and five facts about the ways animals move.
Take your facts from “How Animals Move” and from your own observations.
Use precise unit words such as gallop, spiral, squeeze, signal and suffer.
Lay the facts out as a numbered list so a reader can scan them quickly.
writing.modelText: How Animals Move. 1. A horse can gallop across open grass. 2. A snail travels slowly in a spiral. 3. A cat will squeeze through a narrow gap.
writing.expectedLength: A heading and five numbered facts

items: Heading: How Animals Move
Fact 1: A horse can gallop swiftly across open grass to escape danger.
Fact 2: A snail moves slowly, tracing a spiral shape into its shell as it grows.
Fact 3: A cat can squeeze its flexible body through a narrow gap in a fence.
Fact 4: Birds give a signal to warn the flock when one of them spots danger.
Fact 5: Some animals suffer when there is no water nearby, so they must travel far to find a river or a pool.

writing.successCriteria: Facts are accurate; five unit words are used precisely; the list is numbered; spelling and punctuation are checked
writing.support: Reread the animal text and tick each movement word before you write.
writing.extension: Add a glossary line explaining one movement word in your own words.

writing.title: Writing 5: Proofread and Improve
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Choose the how-to guide or the adventure story you have already written.
Revise three sentences so the verbs and adverbs are accurate.
Add two useful details that a reader would want to know.
Then explain, in one sentence, why one of your changes makes the writing clearer.
writing.modelText: I changed “the horse ran fast” to “the horse galloped quickly past the fence”, because the stronger verb and the adverb show the reader how it moved.
writing.expectedLength: A revised piece plus one explanation sentence

items: Revised sentence 1: 'Then, check that it is not hurt' became 'Then, check gently for any injuries.'
Revised sentence 2: 'After that, offer a little water' became 'After that, offer a little water calmly, so the animal does not feel frightened.'
Revised sentence 3: 'Finally, carry it to an adult helper' became 'Finally, carry it carefully to an adult helper who can look after it.'
New detail 1: Added a line reminding the reader never to chase a frightened animal.
New detail 2: Added the safety line, 'Always fetch an adult before you go near a lost animal.'
I changed 'check that it is not hurt' to 'check gently for any injuries', because the adverb and the more precise noun show the reader exactly how careful to be.

writing.successCriteria: Three sentences are genuinely revised; two new details are added; the explanation names the improvement
writing.support: Read your work aloud and circle every verb before you change anything.
writing.extension: Swap with a partner and suggest one improvement each, kindly.

writing.title: Writing 6: Draw and Caption the Rescue
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Draw Amal, Leo, Nora and Simba at the moment the dog is carried out of the cave.
Write one sentence under your picture describing what is happening.
Use an adjective before each naming word, such as a shivering dog or a narrow tunnel.
Check that your caption is a full sentence with an end mark.
writing.modelText: Nora carries the thin, shivering dog out of the narrow tunnel while Amal holds the torch steady.
writing.sentenceStarter: In my picture, the three children
writing.expectedLength: One picture and one caption sentence

items: Picture description: all three children stand at the mouth of the cave; Nora holds Simba, the thin and shivering dog, while Amal holds up a flickering torch and Leo looks back at the dark tunnel.
Caption: Amal holds the flickering torch high while Nora carries the shivering, thin dog through the narrow tunnel opening.

writing.successCriteria: The picture matches the story; the caption is one full sentence; at least two adjective + noun phrases appear
writing.support: Say your caption aloud before you write it, and count the words.
writing.extension: Write a second caption from Simba’s point of view.

quizzes.question: What does the verb ‘gallop’ mean?
quizzes.options: To stop something from happening. | A sign or message that tells you something. | To run fast on four legs, like a horse. | The feeling of being pushed or stressed by something.
quizzes.correctAnswer: To run fast on four legs, like a horse.

quizzes.question: What does the adjective ‘greedy’ mean?

quizzes.explanation: Talia uses greedy about people who want an animal but will not care for it properly.

quizzes.question: Which sentence puts the verb into the correct past simple form?
quizzes.options: Yesterday she rescue the bird. | Yesterday she rescued the bird. | Yesterday she rescuing the bird. | Yesterday she will rescue the bird.
quizzes.explanation: Yesterday shows the action is finished, so the regular verb rescue takes the -ed ending.

teacherNotes.note: Model every new action verb aloud and check meaning before independent work, then mix written, spoken and acted responses so learners can show understanding in more than one way. Device safety: an adult stays present for every AI-tutor session and for every recording; no learner works alone with the device, and recordings are reviewed by the adult before upload. Give feedback on complete sentences, on evidence quoted from the text, and on the precision of the unit vocabulary.

Suggested tutor prompts, always used with an adult helper sitting alongside the learner.
Vocabulary: ask the tutor to quiz the five moving words, to contrast accelerate with proceed, and to contrast peek with gaze.
Reading: ask the tutor to read “The Lost Goat” aloud slowly and then question the learner on the order of events.
Grammar: ask the tutor why we write she galloped but she did not gallop, and request five more sentences to change into the past.
Writing: ask the tutor to check whether the how-to steps are clear, whether the past tense holds throughout the story, and where an adverb would sharpen a sentence.
Wellbeing: the pressure and suffer prompts can touch on real worries, so the adult helper stays in the conversation and redirects it if the learner becomes uncomfortable.

grownUpGuide.label: Teacher & Parent Guide
grownUpGuide.intro: In this unit, your child works through "Action and Movement" — new words, a grammar focus, and a story. See exactly what they will practise below.

sections.title: 🧭 About this unit (please read first)
sections.body:
Your child is about 8-9 years old and is building on English they already know. So YOU lead this unit alongside them — a teacher in class or a parent at home.

Work in short, regular sessions rather than one long one. Reading together, saying words out loud, and playing with the grammar patterns matter more than getting every answer right first time.

This guide tells you what the unit covers and how to go through it together. The learner's own pages (Reading & story, Grammar, Activities) are what your child works through on screen.

sections.title: 💬 Using the AI Tutor with your child
sections.body:
The AI Tutor is there for extra practice and conversation — a grown-up should still be nearby, especially the first few times.

Ask the tutor to say a word slowly so your child can copy it: "Please say the word 'gallop' slowly."

Ask it to make up a short question using this unit's words, or to listen to your child's sentence and say if it sounds right.

Ask it for one more practice question if your child wants to keep going after the unit is finished.

sections.title: 🌟 Tips for teaching this unit
sections.body:
Keep sessions short and positive. Stop while it is still enjoyable, not after it has become a chore.

Say new words and example sentences out loud yourselves — hearing English spoken, not just reading it, is what builds confidence.

Let your child make mistakes without worrying. Gently model the correct version rather than correcting every slip.

Praise effort and progress, not just correct answers — confidence carries a learner further than perfect grammar at this stage.

sections.title: What Your Child Will Be Able to Do
items: Use strong action verbs to describe how people and animals move.
Tell a story about the past using the past simple tense (played, galloped, rescued, went).
Describe actions with adverbs of manner (quickly, slowly, carefully).
Build clear adjective + noun phrases (a greedy fox, a spiral staircase).
Give instructions with imperatives and use can and must correctly.
Read and understand an adventure story and talk about the choices the characters make.
Write a short how-to guide and a narrative about an exciting event.

sections.title: Words We Will Learn
items: Moving and Going: gallop · accelerate · proceed · spiral · rate
Looking and Watching: peek · gaze · check · signal · describe

sections.title: How to Teach This Unit, Step by Step
sections.body:
Repeat this simple shape over one or two short sessions:

1. Warm-up (2-3 min)
Say hello in English together and ask what your child remembers from the last unit.

2. Learn the words (5-10 min)
Go through Moving and Going, Looking and Watching, Using Your Hands and Body, Helping and Doing the Right Thing, a few words at a time. Say each word, then have your child repeat it and use it in a short sentence.

3. Grammar and practice (5-10 min)
Look at "Past Simple Tense" together and try a few lines of its practice out loud.

4. Story and listening time (5 min)
Read or listen to "The Spiral Cave" together, and enjoy "The Lost Goat (script)" too.

5. Activity time (5-10 min)
Sit with your child and do "Activities 1: Match the Action" together, reading each instruction aloud for them if needed.

6. Wrap-up (2 min)
Ask what they learned today and celebrate with a “Well done!”

sections.title: Simple Check — What to Look For
sections.body: You do not need a test. Just watch for these as you go through the unit together:
items: All twenty Word Wall words ticked in Activities 5, plus five movement verbs used precisely in the Writing 4 fact file.
Grammar practice 1 completed accurately and the Writing 3 cave recount written entirely in the past simple.
Adverbs supplied correctly in Activities 3 and at least three -ly adverbs used in the Speaking 1 recording.
Adjective + noun phrases built in Activities 4 with a / an chosen by sound, and two more in the Writing 6 caption.
Grammar practices 4 and 5 completed, and every step of the Writing 1 guide opening with an imperative verb.
The five story comprehension answers supported by quoted detail, plus a reasoned opinion given in Speaking 5.
A four-step how-to guide and a six-to-ten sentence adventure story, both revised after the Writing 5 proofread.
